html:
With the pandemic, things aren’t looking good in Aachen either. I hope all is well in Aachen and in Europe, and that everyone makes it safely through this troubled spring.

I did my PhD in Aachen.

I’ve gone back every year since graduating, but I still miss my days there: the old town and its streets, the winters with the occasional snowfall, and the springs, summers and falls with their frequent rain.

On the whole, a PhD in Aachen, or in Germany generally, isn’t hard to finish, because there’s no publication requirement. As a result, the quality of PhD graduates varies enormously, and a PhD can take a very, very long time. At my institute there’s a guy who is the most familiar face in the whole university. He started his PhD in 2003 and still hasn’t finished. Granted, he runs his own company and does the PhD part-time, but this is taking “steady” a bit far: a child born the year he started is going to college this year…

The PhD students at the institute are all good, though their publication output is astonishingly low. They do work in a solid, careful way (partly because they’re slow). I learned a lot during my PhD, and I learned a lot from them.

In January 2013, while I was at a winter school in Munich, I came to Aachen for an interview at the acoustics institute I later graduated from. It was my first time in Aachen. I wasn’t sure the interview would work out, so in the hour or so before my train I walked from the station to the RWTH main building, taking a quick photo tour of the town.


A PhD in Germany is different from most countries. There are no junior supervisors, and no assistant or associate professors to guide you. An institute usually has just one or two senior professors, who have no time at all to supervise students, so you have to rely on yourself. As my German colleagues put it, you get ins kalte Wasser schmeissen, thrown into cold water. So you have to plan your time carefully: if you don’t go to the professor, the professor may never come to you. Some colleagues met with the professor only once a year, and while I was at the institute two colleagues ended up leaving without a degree.

German PhD students also take on a lot of teaching: supervising students, running lab courses, setting and grading final exams, helping write proposals or working on the professor’s industry projects, and so on.



Aachen’s electrical engineering faculty has lots of big names, and its students go on to excellent careers. Professor Jens-Rainer Ohm at the institute next door is a giant in communications. I took his Multimedia Communication Systems course, which nearly killed me. Worst of all, the professor speaks in a pure tone, a single frequency, which is extremely hypnotic. The course starts with plenty of students, but attendance gradually dwindles to single digits. His lecture videos are online, so it doesn’t matter if you skip. The problem is that even the videos put you to sleep. To any younger students who are stressed out by their theses and sleeping badly: try his videos. Teasing aside, he is a top-notch professor and a very gentle person.


RWTH has the largest virtual reality environment in the world, the CAVE (I don’t know whether it’s been overtaken since), and our institute was responsible for its acoustic system. Whenever visitors came, we had to go and receive them and give demos.



Every year the institute holds a Christmas party. It’s an acoustics institute, so of course there has to be music; and it’s an acoustics institute, so of course the noise control is excellent and the neighbors are never disturbed: every year the party was held in the anechoic chamber. After the institute moved to its new building, which has no residential area around it, that stopped mattering.




Every year RWTH also holds its own version of The Voice. I can’t remember which year it was, but after the competition ended, the organizers invited people in the audience to come up and sing karaoke while they counted the votes. Nobody went up. Then people started egging on one of the organizing staff to sing, and after some bashful protesting, the guy went up and sang Gary Chaw’s Mandopop hit “Mr. Lonely.” He brought the house down and completely upstaged the contestants. If you were there that day, raise your hand!



The funfair comes twice a year. I went two days before leaving Aachen; maybe I was feeling under the weather, but I nearly threw up afterward.




The university’s two sports halls offer all kinds of activities for free: basketball, volleyball, badminton, aerobics and more. You just register online in advance. What I miss most now are the days when I played ball with my friends every week.






If you like acoustics or want to study it, consider RWTH’s acoustics institute. It’s not only very strong; the professor is good-looking, too.

Which scientists and scholars are brilliant, highly accomplished and good-looking, too?

The range of acoustics courses is very complete, and there are all kinds of lab courses.

To the seniors in acoustics: I want to study acoustics. Can anyone talk me out of it?


I miss my student days, and I’m glad my last years as a student were spent at RWTH, in Aachen.

Fanyu Meng · 108 consultations · rated 5.0 · Zhihu outstanding answerer in acoustics · PhD in acoustics, RWTH Aachen University
